analysis.one_liner: Creates prison terms and pay clawbacks for private equity owners when their cost-cutting harms or kills hospital patients.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in June 2024 by Senator Warren with one cosponsor, never received a vote; it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a crime, punishable by one to six years in prison, for executives and owners at private equity firms whose decisions contribute to a hospital or other health care company collapsing after they take it over — specifically when that collapse leads to a patient's injury or death. It would let the Justice Department and state attorneys general claw back executive pay, dividends, and fees collected up to ten years before such a failure, and use that money to cover unpaid wages and fund pension shortfalls. It would also cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to health care providers that sell their buildings to real estate investment trusts, end certain REIT tax breaks, and require large health care companies to publicly report their ownership, debt, and investor fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients treated at hospitals, nursing homes, and physician practices owned by private equity or heavily indebted health systems, who would gain new protection against the cost-cutting, debt-loading, and asset-stripping that can precede facility closures and patient harm. Health care workers benefit because clawed-back money is earmarked for unpaid salaries, benefit shortfalls, and pension funding. Communities that have seen a local hospital close benefit from the accountability mechanism and the requirement that ownership and debt information be published.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health care workers, and their communities

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime, with one to six years in prison and civil penalties up to five times the clawback amount, for a private equity firm or its executives whose actions contribute to a 'triggering event' — closure, bankruptcy, loan or rent default, or mass unpaid wages — that injures or kills a patient at the acquired company [S2, S3].

Lets the Attorney General and state attorneys general claw back compensation — salaries, bonuses, dividends, monitoring and transaction fees, golden parachutes — received from the acquired company in the ten years before or after the failure, and directs that money to unpaid wages, employee benefit and pension shortfalls, and the health needs of the harmed community [S2, S3].

Bars any entity from receiving Medicare or Medicaid payments if it sells its assets to a real estate investment trust or pledges them as collateral to one — a common structure in health care buyouts where the operating company is left renting its own buildings from investors [S2, S3].

Eliminates two tax advantages for real estate investment trusts holding health care property and strips REIT dividends from the pass-through business income deduction, removing tax subsidies for the landlord model of health care [S2, S3].

Requires hospitals, health systems, physician practices, nursing homes, hospices, dialysis facilities and similar entities to report annually to HHS — with the information posted on a public website — on ownership changes, debt levels, real estate leases, fees and dividends paid to investors, with civil penalties up to $5 million for false or missing reports [S3].

Directs the HHS Inspector General to study and report to Congress on profit-driven practices in health care, including upcoding, understaffing, insurer denial mechanisms, and efforts to evade state bans on corporate ownership of medical practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms and their executives, who would face prison time, clawbacks of up to ten years of compensation, and civil penalties; real estate investment trusts that own health care property, which would lose tax benefits and the ability to have Medicare- and Medicaid-enrolled providers as tenants who sold or pledged assets to them; and health care executives and corporate owners generally, who would face new annual disclosure requirements backed by $5 million penalties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity firms and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The criminal standard attaches to outcomes — a closure, a default, or wages unpaid — that can result from forces beyond an owner's control, such as reimbursement cuts or local market collapse; the bill's affirmative defense (clear and convincing proof the owner could not prevent the event) softens but does not eliminate the risk of punishing investors for a facility's failure rather than their conduct [S3].

Cutting off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell or pledge assets to REITs, and repealing REIT tax benefits, would remove one of the few capital channels available to cash-strapped hospitals and nursing homes that need to sell real estate to stay open, and could chill investment in struggling facilities [S3].

Companies could delay or restructure transactions to avoid the reporting rules, and the compliance burden of annual ownership, debt, and fee disclosures falls on every covered entity, including small physician practices under common control [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability mechanism is aimed at a real and documented problem — private equity deals in health care have repeatedly preceded closures, staffing cuts, and patient harm — and the bill directs any recovered money to the workers and communities who bore the harm, which is well designed. The blunt edges are real: the ban on REIT relationships is a sledgehammer that could cut off capital for facilities that genuinely need it, and a criminal law keyed to outcomes like defaults and closures raises fair-notice concerns, partly mitigated by the affirmative defense. On balance, the benefits to patients and workers outweigh the costs, though the REIT provisions would have benefited from narrower drafting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the Corporate Crimes Against Health Care Act on June 11, 2024, joined by Senator Markey [S3, S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the Senate never debated it, and no vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5, S1].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor, Senator Markey, giving it two Senate supporters out of 100 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity firms, health care REITs, and the executives they pay are better off because the bill died — none of the new criminal liability, clawbacks, payment bans, or tax increases ever took effect, and patients and workers at corporate-owned health facilities gained no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and health care REITs

industries.note: The bill would expose PE executives and funds to prison time, ten-year compensation clawbacks, and civil penalties up to five times the clawback when a leveraged health care acquisition collapses and patients are hurt. Its interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the patients and workers the bill protects.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts in health care
industries.note: REITs would lose their biggest health care customers: any provider selling or pledging assets to a REIT would be barred from Medicare and Medicaid, and REITs would lose two tax benefits for health care property. The bill targets the sale-leaseback model that leaves operating companies paying rent on their own facilities — a structure that can drain the cash hospitals need for care.

industries.industry: Corporate health care owners and executives
industries.note: Hospitals, health systems, physician practices, and other corporate-owned providers would face mandatory annual public disclosure of ownership, debt, real estate deals, and investor fees, with penalties up to $5 million. Executives whose conduct contributes to a triggering patient-harm event could have up to ten years of pay clawed back.
